question: The former director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), Dr Robert Redfield, is heavily critical of the political handling of the COVID-19 vaccine. It was allegedly marketed as a ‘vaccine’ and made mandatory, despite it being clear early on that it did not prevent infection or spread of the virus.

In medical and biological terms, mRna and DNA vaccines qualify as gene therapy; however, they were exempted from the relevant EU legislation in 2009 under pressure from the pharmaceutical lobby. Redfield maintains that the issue behind the development of the vaccine was not science, but rather policy implementation.

He also says that with regard to gene therapy vaccines, it is not known how much spike protein is produced in the body, for how long it is produced or where in the body it is produced following vaccination.1 It has long been reported in scientific literature that people who receive gene therapy vaccines may produce uncontrolled amounts of spike protein years after vaccination. 1.
Why did the Commission bow to pressure from the pharmaceutical lobby in 2009, using EU Directive 2009/120/EC to exempt mRNA and DNA gene therapy vaccines from the relevant EU legislation?
What is the Commission’s view on the remarks of the former CDC director?
What is the Commission doing to ensure that there is finally an investigation into whether all individuals in the EU who received the COVID-19 vaccine continue to produce spike proteins?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (9.4.2026) mRNA vaccines authorised in the EU against COVID-19 are not genetically modified organisms and do not contain genes as their active substance. They are not used with the aim to restore, correct, or modify human genes. Therefore, they are not considered a gene therapy.

mRNA vaccines are biotechnology medicinal products regulated under the EU pharmaceutical legislation to ensure their quality, safety, and efficacy. The definitions and detailed requirements for gene therapy and somatic cell therapy medicinal products were updated in 20091 to take into account scientific and technical progress in the field of advanced therapies, as reflected in Regulation (EC) No 1394/20072.

Hundreds of millions of people worldwide have received the mRNA COVID-19 vaccines. All EU-authorised medicines, including mRNA vaccines, are continuously and rigorously monitored. According to the European Medicines Agency, enhanced monitoring has found no safety issues related to the distribution of vaccine components3.
